episodes.168487: A cluster of strong to severe storms moved through far northeast Missouri and extreme southern Iowa in the early morning hours of June 17th. These brought heavy rain amounts and a few damaging wind gusts.
episodes.168642: As an area of high pressure centered itself to the east of New Mexico, this aided in the development of a monsoon moisture plume across Arizona and western New Mexico on June 16, 2022. The 2022 monsoon season was officially underway, and with the moisture plume focused across the western half of the state, this was generally where thunderstorms developed throughout the afternoon and evening hours. While even the low-levels moistened up, dewpoint depressions were still large enough where the threat for strong downburst winds was a big concern. Shower and thunderstorm activity near Taos produced 60 to 75 mph wind gusts late in the evening. Meanwhile, fire weather season was not done with New Mexico yet as another wildfire was stated in eastern Bernalillo County along Interstate 40 and Carnuel Canyon that forced several evacuation as well as the closure of the Interstate.
episodes.168643: Scattered thunderstorms developed near the mountains, and a lee side surface trough, to the north and then shifted south and organized into a Mesoscale Convective System (MCS) that produced strong damaging winds and some hail across the Midlands of SC, along with locally heavy rain and flooding in the Columbia metropolitan area, in the afternoon and evening.
episodes.168679: Along a plunging cold frontal boundary, a nocturnal complex of thunderstorms tracked to the east-southeast from Illinois into far southwestern central Indiana.  Copious vertical wind shear and instability, including strong mid-level temperature lapse rates, fueled embedded cells with scattered severe winds.
episodes.168688: Thunderstorms developed along a southward moving outflow boundary in Tennessee and arrived in north Alabama during the midday hours. One report of damaging winds was received in Lincoln County.
episodes.168689: Thunderstorms developed along a southward moving outflow boundary in Tennessee and arrived in north Alabama during the midday hours, exiting northwest and north central Alabama by mid afternoon.  Large hail and damaging wind gusts were reported.
episodes.168690: The monsoonal moisture plume continued to be focused across the western half of New Mexico on June 17, 2022. This led to another active day across this area as thunderstorms developed across the high terrain in the early afternoon before becoming more widespread across lower elevations as the day progressed. Steering flow moved this activity in a south to north direction. With improving moisture advection, heavy rainfall was more common with the strongest thunderstorms. While this prompted Flash Flood Warnings for the Cerro Pelado burn scar, no impacts were known. Meanwhile, Albuquerque broke a 78 day streak with no measurable precipitation when thunderstorms finally impacted the metro area. Farther north in Farmington, strong downburst winds were responsible for a 60 mph gust.
episodes.168706: A broken line of supercells formed on the evening of June 16th as a mid-level trough interfered with agitated cumulus clouds in northwestern Ohio and a lake breeze east of Lake Erie. Moderate to high instability and high wind shear, 35-45kts and 1500-2500J/kg, helped with robust convection.

episodes.169035: A north-south stationary boundary bisected central Pennsylvania ahead of a cold front approaching from the Great Lakes on June 16, 2022. A broken line of showers and thunderstorms formed along a lake-breeze front that developed over northwestern Pennsylvania, just ahead of the approaching cold front. As this line progressed southeastward, one of the cells within the line became a long-track supercell that produced a swath of wind damage and hail from Warren County southeastward to the Lower Susquehanna Valley.
episodes.169045: As a heat wave ensued across the Central Appalachians during the middle of June, the atmosphere remained primed for afternoon showers and thunderstorms. On June 16th, the strongest storms resided across the northern portions of West Virginia, where numerous trees were blown down and quarter sized hail fell. A few instances of heavy downpours within the storms occurred, leading to high water along local roadways in Tyler and Gilmer Counties.
episodes.169055: Afternoon showers and thunderstorms quickly got underway across southeast Ohio on June 16th as abnormally warm temperatures were in place. A few storms grew to become strong to severe, resulting in damaging winds that knocked down trees in the towns of Reinersville and Lower Salem. Heavy downpours were also observed within activity that afternoon, which caused flash flooding to be observed along the Duck Creek and Lower Muskingum River in Washington County.

Numerous trees were blown down across the central portions of West Virginia from strong wind gusts in the early afternoon, followed by more trees down in the southeastern portions of the state a few hours later. The most significant damage caused by these storms was a roof being blown off of a home in Lincoln County. Heavy downpours and antecedent wet ground conditions also resulted in one instance of flash flooding along sections of Route 129 and 39 in the town of Poe.

episodes.169232: An organized complex of thunderstorms moved southeast across southern Illinois during the early morning hours. The leading edge of the storms was accompanied by strong winds, which resulted in areas of wind damage. The damaging winds were fairly widespread north of the Marion/Carbondale area. Places from Du Quoin and Mount Vernon east to Mount Carmel and Carmi reported pockets of significant wind damage, including roof damage and downed trees and power poles. Further south, damage was mainly confined to isolated tree damage. The combination of mid-level dry air and very moist low levels, characterized by surface dew points in the 70's, produced strong downdrafts. Although deep-layer wind shear was generally less than 25 knots, the established cold pool with the storm complex sustained the surface gust front. An upper-level ridge across the Plains and a trough over the Northeast produced a northwest wind flow that steered early-day thunderstorm clusters into the lower Ohio Valley.
episodes.169239: An organized complex of thunderstorms moved south-southeast across western Kentucky during the early to mid-morning hours. The leading edge of the storms was accompanied by strong winds, which resulted in pockets of minor wind damage. The minor damage mainly consisted of downed tree limbs and isolated downed trees. The combination of mid-level dry air and very moist low levels, characterized by surface dew points in the 70's, produced strong downdrafts. Although deep-layer shear was generally less than 25 knots, the established cold pool with the storm complex sustained the organized gust front. An upper-level ridge across the Plains and a trough over the Northeast produced a northwest wind flow that steered early-day thunderstorm clusters into the lower Ohio Valley.
episodes.169280: An organized complex of thunderstorms moved east-southeast across southwest Indiana during the early to mid-morning hours. The biggest swath of tree damage was across the Evansville metro area, where lots of small tree limbs and several whole trees were blown down. episodes.169918: A stationary front was located north of the state heading into the day on June 17th, before transitioning to a slow moving cold front that continued to near the state throughout the day. Eastern KY's placement in the warm sector, combined with ample moisture advection from the Gulf of Mexico, set the stage for shower and thunderstorm development. Storms developed to our west, over western and central Kentucky, and began to impact eastern Kentucky by just after noon. Strong winds aloft resulted in wind damage at the surface, as well as decent storm motions. Most of the storms had exited the state just 2 to 3 hours later. Some of the strongest storms brought widespread downed trees and power lines and caused damage to buildings and home around eastern Kentucky. In total, 121 storm reports of damage were sent out as a result of this storm system.
episodes.169966: A line of thunderstorms became severe and produced numerous reports of wind damage as it moved southward through Eastern NC during the evening hours.
episodes.169992: Remnants of a mesoscale convective system moved across the northern portions of the Mid-South. This produced an outflow boundary that moved south into north Mississippi. It was the focus for severe thunderstorms that produced large hail and damaging wind.

A strong upper level disturbance then began to cross the region during the afternoon. Thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon. An isolated severe thunderstorm produced large hail in the vicinity of Easton in northeast Aroostook county.
episodes.170144: A cold front encroaching the Ohio Valley on the afternoon of June 17th ran into favorable conditions for strong to severe thunderstorms thanks to abnormally warm temperatures and sufficient low level moisture. Multiple instances of downed trees were observed throughout Lawrence County in response to damaging wind gusts. Heavy downpours, coupled with previous rainfall from days prior, led to Duck Creek and the Little Muskingum River rising out of their banks through the evening hours of the 17th and into the next day. This resulted in minor flooding along adjacent local roads.
episodes.170148: A cold front sweeping through the area on June 17th was aided by abnormally warm temperatures and low level moisture to help spark afternoon showers and thunderstorms across eastern Kentucky. Several of these storms grew to be strong to severe, resulting in downed trees and power lines from damaging wind gusts. One particular storm also yielded golf ball sized hail in the town of Fallsburg in Lawrence County.
episodes.170149: On the afternoon of June 17th, a cold front made its way through the Ohio Valley into the Central Appalachians. The boundary encroached on an area where abnormally warm temperatures were underway, which aided in shower and thunderstorm development. As convection passed through Dickenson County, strong wind gusts resulted in downed trees and power lines in the town of Russell Mart.
episodes.170150: A strong nocturnal low-level jet interacting with a nearly stationary frontal boundary triggered a Mesoscale Convective System (MCS) over northern Missouri during the pre-dawn hours of June 17th.  The large thunderstorm cluster tracked east-southeastward along the boundary, producing significant wind damage and flash flooding.  The storms were focused along and southeast of a Rushville...to Springfield...to Shelbyville...to Robinson line.  Numerous trees and power lines were blown down.  In addition, very heavy rainfall of 3 to 5 inches along and south of a Jacksonville to Effingham line created pockets of flash flooding.
episodes.170500: A thunderstorm became severe as it moved into northeastern Johnson County.
episodes.170566: In the late afternoon, two boundaries, one from the north and one from the south, began colliding near the I-70 corridor. This collision caused thunderstorms to begin forming along the I-70 corridor. One of these storms created hail up to a quarter in size.
episodes.170713: Dissipating thunderstorms moving northeast out of northern Colorado produced destructive outflow winds over portions of the southern Nebraska Panhandle. Measured wind gusts around 60 mph were observed while trained spotters estimated higher speeds. Damage south of Scottsbluff included four snapped wooden power poles and an overturned farm pivot.
episodes.170732: Several rounds of severe thunderstorms moved through areas of northern Missouri, into central Missouri. The storms went well into the overnight hours producing scattered instances of damaging winds, along with a few marginally severe hailstones.
episodes.170782: Scattered severe thunderstorms associated with a warm front produced damaging winds, large hail, and three tornadoes across portions of central Virginia.
episodes.170843: On the morning of June 17th, a very warm and humid air mass was present across southern Indiana as a cold front extended west to east across central Illinois into central Indiana. South of the cold front, a Mesoscale Convective System moved across southern Indiana during the mid-morning hours, with storms feeding off the large amounts of instability. Across southern Indiana, the main observed severe hazard was damaging winds, with wind damage being observed across several counties.
episodes.170861: Scattered thunderstorms developed over western North Carolina during the afternoon. Several of the storms produced brief severe weather in the form of damaging wind gusts.
episodes.170862: Scattered thunderstorms developed over upstate South Carolina during the afternoon. Several of the storms produced brief severe weather in the form of damaging wind gusts and large hail.
episodes.170985: Severe thunderstorms produced large hail across parts of Boulder, Larimer and Weld counties.  The hail ranged from quarter to ping pong ball size.
episodes.171013: On the morning of June 17th, a warm and humid air mass was present across central Kentucky, with temperatures in the upper 70s and lower 80s and dewpoints in the low-to-mid 70s. A weak, decaying cold front was positioned to the north of the region across central Indiana and merely served to guide storms from west to east across the region. During the mid-to-late morning hours, a Mesoscale Convective System moved from west to east across the region, feeding off high instability to produce strong-to-severe thunderstorms across much of central Kentucky. While wind damage from thunderstorm outflow was the main observed severe hazard with these storms, some severe hail was also observed.
episodes.171055: Multiple rounds of storms developed along a stationery/retreating front resulting in numerous hail reports near Lincoln and Seward several hours apart. More isolated hail and wind reports were received other areas in southeast Nebraska.
